The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres, on curves cut into the mountainside, and the Hollin, its steam engine since 1932, still makes the climb every morning. When the line was built in 1911, its builders kept a herd of goats at Gessen, the halfway halt, for their milk, and the herd's descendants still treat the halt as their own.

The water tank at Gessen no longer fills the engine, which takes on water at Pell, but its pipe still drips onto the rails, and the goats come down off the scree slope to drink from the puddle between them. When we arrived, Tomas Brede's grandson was crouched by the overflow pool beside the track; he had just pulled a trout from it, and a single scale still glittered on his thumb as three goats pushed their noses in beside him. The train waits at Gessen until the goats have had enough and wander off the rails.

Ilse Marran sounds the whistle twice, and the goats lift their dripping beards to look at her before going back to the puddle. The visitors who came up to photograph the viaduct over the Lenn gorge spend the halt photographing goats instead. When the last goat finally stepped off the sleepers, a passenger behind me laughed out loud, and I laughed with him most of the way to the viaduct.

The rest of the climb keeps good time. The stone wall below the scree slope, rebuilt in 2017 and paid for by the council itself, holds the loose rock firmly. The farmers' cheese from the high farms is loaded at Tarsel and goes down on the dawn train, a trade the timetable is built around, and the visitors come up afterwards; in winter the snowploughs keep the village road open. In the council's timetable every station has its minute except Gessen, beside which there is only a small printed goat.

At Tarsel I bought a copy of that timetable at the ticket window, goat and all, and I still laugh whenever I unfold it.

passage:
Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to keep the tiles. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost the most and take the longest to build, two full summers. But the other designs left the diving tower to be pulled down for want of money, and Lind's paid for its repair by selling the old tiles.

The tiles were lifted and sold one by one to members of the swimming club. The floor of the new basin is plain white. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the terrace, the pumps sit beneath the terrace, and the café by the north gate has walls of timber from the old changing cubicles. The tower, repaired with the club's money, still stands, and a flood wall runs between the basin and the river. I have seen the pike's tail behind a kitchen sink in Mill Lane and one of its eyes set into a garden path, and it is hard to picture a happier retirement for a fish.

On opening day every changing cubicle had a bar of soap stamped with a pike, and children carried them home like prizes.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. This summer the club posed on the same steps to take the picture again, each member holding a tile, so that the pike could lie whole on the terrace in front of them.

It came out with two heads, because the Pell sisters had each bought what she was sure was the head, and the photographer laughed so hard he had to start again. I laughed with him, and so did everyone on the steps, both Pell sisters included.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. In May the council ordered enough paint to give all seven the same green, and they came out saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine.

Here is how it happened. Every spring the city's inspectors mark each bridge with a dab of coloured chalk, a different colour for each span, so that their reports can name a bridge by colour instead of a number; they also ring any cracks they find. The work order told the parks crew to paint each bridge in its marked colour, meaning the green swatch clipped to the order. The crew found seven dabs of chalk and matched every one, sending to the depot for the extra shades as they went.

By the time anyone looked at the order again, four bridges were finished and people were stopping on them to stare. The bronze sentry who has stood at the middle of the lime bridge since 1971 now rests his hand on a rifle with a tangerine stock, because an inspector once tagged the gun instead of the railing. I grin every time I cross that bridge and see him standing guard in his new colours.

When the mix-up came to light, residents phoned all week asking to keep the colours, and Councillor Mara Varga's online vote to name the bridges was won easily by Plum, Lime, Teal and the rest. A class at Larch Street School has since worked out that the colours nearly match the bus lines at the far ends, so people can tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and the class now explains its scheme to visitors who come down to the river. The two cracks the inspectors had ringed were repaired first, at no extra cost, and a week of rain only delayed the paint on the concrete.

Of all the stories this city tells about itself, this is the one I most enjoy: seven bridges painted the colours of a box of chalk because one line of a work order was followed exactly as written.

passage:
Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that riders grip their handlebars until their knuckles show white, which is how the bend came to be named the Knuckle.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill, and before the start he asked Hettie to keep the top line of the results board clear for Jory.

Arlo led from the stone bridge, past the old chapel, up the Knuckle and beyond the war memorial, and Jory passed him only within sight of the green. Hettie stopped the clock at 9:41, the champion's first winning time to the very second, set thirty-eight years earlier, and Arlo threw his cap into the air. Nell Odrey finished third. Of all the seconds a two-kilometre climb could take, the boy had found the exact one Arlo found in 1988, and I grinned all the way back down the lane.

By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. The winner's cake comes from a ring of grandmothers who choose its flavour in secret each spring, and this year they chose ginger, the favourite of both Jory and Arlo. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

I have watched the climb for twenty years, and the hill has yet to hand out a happier coincidence than two riders, thirty-eight years apart, tied to the very second.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran inherited an old machine from her uncle and kept it in its case, untouched, booklet tucked inside the lid. The keys had stopped working, clogged with forty years of eraser crumbs. Dad offered the oil from the garage and said I would manage. My cousin Juno, who saw the typewriter for the first time that evening, asked whether I had thought of the poetry contest instead.

March 4. Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street, had a line of customers and could spare me only a minute. He sold me a brush for cleaning out the keys, and I paid the price on its tag. Then he tapped one line of my entry form: the deadline was the day entries had to arrive, he said, so mine would have to be in the post by Monday, four days sooner than I had planned. He wanted me out before his next customer, and to him the typewriter was one more old machine.

March 5. I did the rest on my own. I cleared the crumbs row by row with the brush, threaded Gran's spare ribbon from the case, and checked the carriage spring, which still pulled firmly. Juno made capital of every jam, reporting each one to Aunt Rhea at dinner as proof the machine was hopeless.

March 7. Juno came over, still sure I would give up before Monday. I had just typed my opening sentence when she reached past my shoulder and jabbed at the keys, and I told her straight out that she had already jammed the e twice that morning and had no right to touch the machine again.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, the day Mr. Ostrow said it had to go. Juno had to ask me who Mr. Ostrow was. She is a year past the contest's age limit, and she says she would sooner borrow a pen than that machine. When Gran asked who had cleaned the keys, I told her I had done it alone.
